mcqs.question: How do you represent a building spanning x=2 to x=6 with height 5 as sweep-line events for the Skyline problem?
options: A single event at x=2 with height 5
An event at x=2 removing height 5 from the active set and an event at x=6 adding it
A start event at x=2 adding height 5 to the active set, and an end event at x=6 removing height 5 from the active set
Two events at x=6, one adding and one removing height 5
mcqs.explanation: The building's height joins the active set at its left edge and leaves at its right edge, mirroring the start/end event decomposition from sweep line generally. Swapping which edge adds versus removes, or placing both events at the same x, breaks the sweep entirely.

mcqs.question: In the event-sweep-with-max-heap implementation, why must the heap store (height, end-x) pairs rather than just heights?
options: So the heap can be sorted by end-x instead of height
Because a heap can only hold tuples, never plain numbers
So a stale entry — a height whose building has already ended — can be identified and lazily discarded once its end-x has passed the current sweep position
To convert the max-heap into a min-heap
mcqs.explanation: A binary heap can't delete an arbitrary middle element efficiently, so ended buildings are left in place and identified later by comparing their stored end-x against the current sweep position, then popped off the top before reading the max. Storing only the height would make that check impossible.

mcqs.question: The max-heap in the Skyline sweep still contains a height whose building ended several events ago. What's the standard fix?
options: Rebuild the heap from scratch at every event
Switch to a min-heap so old entries sink toward the bottom
Increase the heap's capacity so stale entries don't cause an overflow
Lazily pop entries off the top of the heap whenever their stored end-x is less than or equal to the current sweep position, before reading the current max
mcqs.explanation: This is lazy deletion: since a heap can only cheaply remove its top, stale entries are left in place and cleared just before they'd matter, by checking and popping from the top until a genuinely active entry surfaces. Rebuilding the whole heap every event would work but destroys the O(n log n) bound.

mcqs.question: At the same x-coordinate, one building starts and a different, shorter building ends. Why must the start event be processed before the end event at that tied x?
options: It doesn't matter, since both events happen at the same instant
Processing the end first guarantees the tallest key point is always found
Start events must always be sorted alphabetically before end events
If the ending building isn't the tallest, the max is already updated by the new building before the shorter one's removal, so no spurious dip is ever reported at that x
mcqs.explanation: Processing starts before ends at a tie means any height change from a new arrival is folded into the active set before an unrelated departure is processed, avoiding a momentary incorrect key point that doesn't reflect the true silhouette. Getting the order backwards can insert a dip the skyline never actually had.

mcqs.question: How does the Skyline problem differ from Meeting Rooms II, given both use a similar start/end event sweep?
options: Skyline needs the actual maximum active height at each event, not just a count of how many buildings are currently active
Skyline doesn't require sorting events, unlike Meeting Rooms II
Meeting Rooms II uses a max-heap of heights while Skyline uses two sorted arrays
Skyline only needs to track whether the active set is empty or non-empty
mcqs.explanation: Meeting Rooms II only needs the size of the active set, trackable with a plain counter. Skyline needs the maximum value among the active set's contents, which requires a max-heap (or ordered structure) instead of a counter — the rest of the sweep skeleton, sorting and scanning events, is identical.

mcqs.question: A mapping/GIS system needs to compute the combined outline of thousands of overlapping building footprints for rendering. Which technique is this closest to?
options: A nested-loop pairwise intersection test between every pair of footprints
Sweep line with a max-heap of active heights, the same mechanism used to solve the Skyline problem
A hash map keyed by footprint ID counting how many footprints overlap it
Binary search over the footprints sorted by area
mcqs.explanation: Computing a combined silhouette from many overlapping regions is exactly the Skyline problem's shape, and the same event-sweep-with-max-heap approach scales to thousands of footprints at O(n log n), where a pairwise check would be quadratic and infeasible per frame.
